paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And what Lam Rim teaches us is: extraordinary is not the things that we normally think are extraordinary. They are the small kindnesses that we do each and every day to help other people. That's what's extraordinary. Because most people don't spend the time even thinking about the kind things that could be done during the day. So your extraordinary doesn't have to be a $250 million company. Your extraordinary could be a house where people don't fight with each other, or an office where people collaborate and celebrate each other's gifts together, and reach toward a common vision, and do it together, and support each other in the good and the bad. That's extraordinary. Extra-ordinary. Not ordinary.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And the Lam Rim is also extremely cool. Like I said, it's enlightenment for dummies. But the Lam Rim contains the essence of the open and secret teachings all in one. So it's not really "enlightenment for dummies." People are like, "Oh, I need the 18 ACI courses. They're the more intellectual ones. They're the real thing." Really? I don't think so. In fact, the Lam Rim is considered the preparation for the Diamond Way — because it is a practice that changes your heart. It changes your mind and it changes your heart.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So which one should you do? Should you do the 18 courses, or should you do the Lam Rim? I hear— {\~ two fast thunder}. Both. Okay.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But you may find one is easier for you than another. Your mind and your heart might be more attracted to different types of practices and different modes.

chapters.title: The four lineages and skillful means

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: When you look at the four primary lineages of Tibetan Buddhism, you have the Gelugpas, you have the Nyingma, you have the Sakya, and you have the — that fourth one just fell out of my head. If someone can remember, put it in the chat.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So each of those lineages has the same goal, different types of practices, different types of methods, different emphases. Different minds, different people need different things at different times too. Why do we teach the Medicine Buddha? Because sometimes we just need a practice that's about compassion. Why do we teach pramana, logic? Because sometimes you need your brain to work through the logic of everything. Why do we need the Guide to the Bodhisattva's Way of Life? Why do we need Abhidharma? Why do we need mind only? Because different people need different things at different times.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And part of being a teacher is also loading up your toolbox for all the different types of beings and all the different people you're going to help. Let's say you meet someone and they're like, "Hey, can you come into my business?" And you're like, "Well, I need to do something from Lam Rim, and I can't call it Lam Rim, so I'm going to call it something else. And I might have to modify it a little bit so the message is clear. And I'm not going to call it Buddhism, and I'm not going to call it meditation. Maybe we'll call it contemplations, or we'll call it daily reflections, or I don't know."

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: I think all this Lam Rim teaches us to become skillful — tab-ke [THABS MKHAS], use skillful means. It teaches us to take what's arising in front of you and to be able to serve whatever appears to you. And if you only know ACI 13 and logic — that's a good question, I'll answer it in a second — if you only know logic, then you're not going to be able to help all people. Because I'm sorry, when I'm having an emotional moment, do not throw logic in my face. I need to be heard. I need to be validated, and I need to be understood. Then you can work on me. Then you can be like, "Well, why don't we take a breath, Tim? Let's take 10 breaths. Let's breathe together. You need to calm down. Your heart rate's way up." Pissed off. Okay, 10 breaths.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Is 10 breaths going to get you to enlightenment? No. But I needed it. And that student needed 10 breaths. "Oh, look, this will just pass. Things will change." Is that emptiness? No. Is it helpful? Yes. Is it true that everything changes? Yes. Is that true in Buddhism? Yes. Is that emptiness? No. But it's helpful. And so Lam Rim teaches you to be helpful.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: Not to ask, "But isn't this against passing on a lineage correctly?" And I didn't say that. We are going to pass on the lineage of Lam Rim correctly. And there is a lineage — which, thank you, Subhuti, for getting to my next topic. In a second. We have to pass on lineages correctly. And as you study Gautama's words and study everything that's been taught, you begin to see that there are no contradictions in the lineages. There's a reason why everything gets said. And that's ACI 15, by the way, if anyone cares.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: But how do we serve other people? How do we make it real right now? That's our concern in Lam Rim: how do we make it applicable to our life right now? And then — the funny question here about "aren't we passing on a lineage?" — I'm like, "Yeah, we're going to pass on that lineage. I'm going to teach this directly from the Tibetan." So you guys are going to get kind of the old way of teaching, but we're going to be mixing them together. We're going to be mixing the Tibetan with the translation, and then we're going to be talking about: how do we live it? What is this really saying?

chapters.title: Take your time — a multi-year course

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: So there are actually several goals of this class. And this is going to be — relax, everybody. Be relaxed. We're not going to finish the Lam Rim in 10 days. We're not going to finish the Lam Rim in 20 days, 20 classes, or 30 classes. We're going to take our time and just relax. I'm in and out of the classes. If you can attend, you can attend. If you can't attend, watch them later.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: What we're going to try to do is give practices to be able to have those realizations that are in the Lam Rim. One of the styles of this Lam Rim is called a nyam-tri [NYAMS KHRID], which means advice through personal experience — instructions in personal experience. So the old way of doing this is we do a step on the path — one of the steps on the path, that's what Lam Rim means, steps on the path — let's say death meditation. Realizing your utter impermanence. And the traditional way would be: we learn all about death, all about the impermanence of you, and then we go into retreat on death meditation. And then we don't continue on to the next step until everyone has the direct realization of their own impermanence. I don't know how to measure that. But the idea is that we're going to be giving the practices as we go through the course itself.

paragraphs.speaker: Timothy Lowenhaupt
paragraphs.text: And what I mean by "course" is — I don't know, this could be five years. It could be 10 years. I don't know. Good luck. Geshe Michael is still finishing the book we're going to be studying. We're about 95% of the way done. So I feel like we can start from the beginning again, because we'll never catch up at the same speed. We have plenty of time. And then, after he finishes the book we're studying, he's going to move on to the Lam Rim Chenmo, Je Tsongkapa's great book — the Lam Rim from which Pabongka Rinpoche draws his course — and he's going to be teaching us the emptiness chapter. So that's going to be coming up in the next year or two. So we've got plenty of time, guys. Relax.
